analysis.one_liner: Lets shooting victims sue negligent gun makers, sellers, and dealers, and recover public costs.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: after being introduced on March 10, 1999, it was sent to the House Judiciary Committee, which took no action on it for the rest of the two-year Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have created a new right to sue in federal court for anyone hurt by a gun that crossed state lines, if the manufacturer, distributor, or retailer had been negligent in making, distributing, or selling it. It also would have let victims sue on behalf of their state and city to recover the medical and police costs that gun violence forces taxpayers to pay. It never got past the committee stage.
analysis.who_benefits: People injured by firearms and families of those killed, who would gain a federal court path to sue negligent gun makers, distributors, and retailers for damages. State and local governments would also benefit, because public money spent on medical care and law enforcement after shootings could be recovered from the industry when negligence was proven.

how_it_helps.text: Anyone damaged by the discharge of a firearm that had been in interstate commerce could bring a civil action in U.S. district court against a manufacturer, distributor, or retailer that was negligent in its manufacture, distribution, or sale.

Victims could also sue on behalf of their state and local government to recover the medical and law enforcement costs of gun violence, with those damages paid directly to the state or political subdivision.
The bill was introduced in the House on March 10, 1999 by Rep. Rod Blagojevich.

analysis.who_pays: Firearm manufacturers, distributors, and retailers, who would face a new federal route to lawsuits and damages whenever negligence in making, distributing, or selling a gun caused harm.

drawbacks.text: The bill would allow suits even when the firearm itself functioned as designed, since the standard is negligence in manufacture, distribution, or sale rather than a defect — courts and juries would have to sort out how far responsibility for a lawfully sold gun extends, and the industry argued this kind of liability could push makers and dealers out of business.
The bill was introduced with only one cosponsor and never advanced, so it received no committee review, hearings, or floor debate in which its costs and design could have been examined and improved.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For victims and taxpayers, the upside was a clear new legal remedy: negligent sellers and makers could be made to pay for the harm and public costs their products caused. The cost falls on the firearms industry, and the strongest objection is that broad liability for lawfully made, lawfully sold guns is hard to calibrate — a defect standard is clear, but negligence in 'distribution or sale' reaches conduct like selling into illegal channels, which courts would have had to define case by case. The bill never got the hearing process where those questions could have been worked out.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee never held a markup or sent it to the floor, so it died when the Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Rep. Rod Blagojevich introduced the Firearms Industry Responsibility Enforcement Act in the House on March 10, 1999.
The bill was referred the same day to the House Committee on the Judiciary, which was its only committee assignment.
The bill attracted one cosponsor, a House Democrat.
No further action appears in the record — no hearing, markup, or vote — and the bill expired when the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Firearm manufacturers, distributors, and retailers were better off, because the bill that would have exposed them to federal lawsuits and public-cost recovery claims never advanced. Victims of gun violence and the state and local governments that pay the medical and policing bills got nothing.

for.name: Rep. Rod Blagojevich
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to create federal suits against negligent gun makers and sellers and to let victims recover public costs for state and local governments.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day it was introduced and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: National Rifle Association
against.what_they_did: Strongly opposed lawsuits against the firearms industry in this era and backed congressional efforts to shield gun makers from such suits, which eventually became law in 2005.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and its single cosponsor were both House Democrats; no Republican support appears in the record, and the Republican-run committee never acted on it.

industries.note: The bill would have given shooting victims a federal court route to sue them for negligence and would have let states and cities recover their medical and law enforcement costs from the industry. Its defeat left the industry free of this federal liability framework.

industries.industry: Hospitals, emergency care, and health insurers
industries.note: The bill targeted the public and medical costs that flow from shootings; without it, those costs stay with hospitals, insurers, and taxpayers instead of being recovered from negligent sellers. The connection is indirect, since the bill would have routed recovery to governments rather than to medical providers.
